classification.difficultyReason: Compare software plots, then use the supplied change-of-base hint to identify a decreasing positive multiplier and explain why it makes the curves flatter.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Use graphing software to sketch the family of functions $y=\log_b(x)$ for $b=2,3,4,5$.

answer.short: All four curves increase, pass through $(1,0)$ and have vertical asymptote $x=0$.
answer.worked: Plot the four functions on the same axes and label each by its base. Each curve passes through $(1,0)$ and through $(b,1)$ for its own base $b$. All four approach the $y$-axis from the right.

spec.description: One set of axes with four labelled logarithmic curves. Blue identifies base 2, red identifies base 3, green identifies base 4 and black identifies base 5. Line styles and matched leader segments distinguish the adjacent curves.
spec.mathematics: All four curves have domain x > 0, intercept (1,0) and asymptote x = 0. For x > 1, the curves are ordered from highest to lowest by bases 2, 3, 4, 5. The order reverses for 0 < x < 1.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Explain how changing the value of $b$ affects the shape of the curve.

answer.short: As $b$ increases, the graph becomes less steep.
answer.worked: For these bases, increasing $b$ compresses the graph vertically towards the $x$-axis. The curve still passes through $(1,0)$ and becomes less steep.

inlines.text: How could this have been deduced algebraically
Think about the change of base formula.

answer.short:
As $b$ increases above $1$, the vertical scale factor $\dfrac{1}{\ln(b)}$ decreases.

By change of base, $\log_b(x)=\dfrac{1}{\ln(b)}\ln(x)$, so the curve moves closer to the $x$-axis.
answer.worked:
By change of base,

$$\begin{align*}\log_b(x)&=\dfrac{\ln(x)}{\ln(b)}\\\log_b(x)&=\dfrac{1}{\ln(b)}\,\ln(x).\end{align*}$$

For $b>1$, $\ln(b)$ is positive and increases as $b$ increases. The positive scale factor $\dfrac{1}{\ln(b)}$ therefore decreases, compressing the curve vertically. For $x>1$, the heights decrease towards zero. For $0<x<1$, the negative heights increase towards zero. At $x=1$, the height stays zero.
